The Picture of Dorian Gray. Oscar Wilde's 1890 philosophical novel tells the story of Dorian Gray, a young man of exceptional beauty who becomes obsessed with preserving his youth and indulges in sensual excess. He makes a pact—his portrait will age while he remains eternally beautiful—and the consequence of his moral decay becomes visible only in the painting's corruption. It is a haunting meditation on beauty, morality, and the price of hedonism.

Published as a short story in 1890 and expanded to a novel in 1891, the work deepened the philosophical resonance of Wilde's vision. Wilde coined the phrase "art for art's sake"—the aesthetic philosophy that dominates the novel through the character of Lord Henry Wotton, who argues that morality is irrelevant to beauty.

The central bargain is this: Dorian wishes his portrait to bear the marks of aging and sin while he remains untouched. The supernatural mechanism through which this occurs is never explained, leaving it ambiguous and darkly magical. Dorian's trajectory moves from innocence, seduced by Lord Henry's nihilism, through hedonistic indulgence to murder and spiritual corruption. All of this remains invisible to the world until the painting reveals the truth.

The novel contains some of Wilde's most famous aphorisms. He writes: "There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book. Books are well written, or badly written. That is all." The portrait's corruption parallels Dorian's moral descent. By the novel's end, the painting is so grotesque it serves as a confessional mirror he cannot escape. In the ending, Dorian's futile attempt to destroy the portrait results in his own death, leaving observers to wonder whether redemption and truth were always possible.
